steps.title: Key Concept
steps.body: Geographical enquiry is a structured investigation into a geographical question or issue. It follows a clear sequence: Question → Hypothesis → Data Collection → Data Presentation → Analysis → Conclusion → Evaluation. AQA requires two fieldwork investigations: one in a physical environment and one in a human environment.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A research question is an open-ended question that guides your enquiry. It should be specific, measurable, and linked to geographical theory.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A hypothesis is a testable statement that predicts the expected outcome of the enquiry. It is often based on geographical theory and can be supported or rejected by evidence.

steps.title: Key Concept
steps.body: You must choose data collection methods that are appropriate for your hypothesis. The evidence should be sufficient, relevant, and reliable. Consider both primary data (collected by you) and secondary data (collected by others).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain the difference between a research question and a hypothesis. | Write a suitable hypothesis for a study investigating how river characteristics change downstream. | Describe three factors you would consider when choosing a fieldwork location.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: You must know your own fieldwork in detail - the examiner will ask about YOUR specific investigation Be able to state your hypothesis clearly and explain the geographical theory behind it Know exactly where your fieldwork took place (named locations, grid references) Be prepared to explain and justify your data collection methods Risk assessment is a common exam question - know specific hazards and mitigations for your environment Remember you need TWO fieldwork investigations: one physical, one human Practice explaining why each method was chosen - link it to your hypothesis
